market_summary:
US equities just experienced their first meaningful shakeout of the year after an extended run of record highs driven by artificial intelligence and megacap growth, leaving investors debating whether the past week’s damage is a healthy reset or the start of something more structural.[8][12][31] Index-level data underline the severity of the move: the S&P 500 fell roughly mid‑single digits from its recent record close, with a single‑session decline of about 2.6% on Friday alone, while the tech‑heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped more than 4% that day as semiconductor and AI‑linked names saw some of their sharpest selling in years.[20][30] Even after the selloff, the S&P 500’s latest available close around 7,405 still sits not far below all‑time highs, while the Nasdaq Composite remains elevated near 25,700, underscoring how far the market has run on the AI theme over the past several quarters.[1][2][8] The Dow Jones Industrial Average has held up somewhat better given its more balanced sector mix, with the most recent reading near 50,867 still reflecting strong 12‑month gains, but beneath the surface leadership has narrowed and volatility has begun to rise meaningfully.[3][30]

The fulcrum for this week’s risk‑off turn was a sharp reversal in the AI and semiconductor complex following months of persistent inflows and multiple expansion, catalyzed by mixed reactions to earnings and guidance from key enablers of the AI infrastructure build‑out.[18][20][31] After setting fresh records early in the week on the back of strong results and guidance from select AI beneficiaries like Marvell Technology and Hewlett Packard Enterprise, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index suddenly dropped more than 10% on Friday, wiping roughly a trillion dollars in market value from AI‑linked names and sparking a broader de‑risking across growth equities.[18][20][30][31] High‑beta chipmakers such as Micron, Broadcom, Advanced Micro Devices, and Marvell saw single‑day declines in the mid‑ to high‑single digits, and the selling bled into software, cybersecurity, and other crowded AI‑related trades.[20][26][31] While there was some evidence of dip‑buying in index futures and large‑cap ETFs at the start of this week, the tenor of flows and commentary suggests that many fast‑money players have begun to reduce exposure and re‑evaluate position sizing rather than reflexively buying every dip.[31][33]

Macro developments simultaneously turned less friendly for risk assets, with a stronger‑than‑expected US payrolls report adding to a run of resilient activity data and sticky inflation, forcing markets to reprice the path of Federal Reserve policy toward a more entrenched "higher‑for‑longer" stance.[13][28][30] May payrolls rose by about 172,000 versus consensus near 88,000, while the unemployment rate ticked higher but remained historically low and the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the PCE price index, is running noticeably above the central bank’s target.[28][30] Policy rates are currently anchored in a 3.50%–3.75% range after a modest easing cycle that began in late 2025, but futures now imply less than a 10% chance of any rate cuts for the remainder of 2026, and some probability that the next move could even be a hike if inflation or growth surprise to the upside.[13] Goldman Sachs Research has pushed its forecast for the next rate cuts out to mid‑2027, emphasizing that resilient employment and activity data raise the bar for additional easing and leave the Fed more tolerant of restrictive policy so long as financial conditions do not tighten disorderly.[14][30]

Geopolitics and commodities added another layer of risk to the equity narrative as renewed conflict in the Middle East drove oil prices sharply higher and reawakened investors’ concerns about a second‑round inflation shock just as the Fed is trying to guide price growth back toward target.[30][31] Brent crude prices have moved toward the high‑double‑digit range per barrel, supported by reports of resumed hostilities between Iran and Israel and uncertainty over potential disruptions to production or transport routes.[30] This has supported energy equities and related cyclicals at the margin, but from a cross‑asset perspective it tightens the policy trade‑off, as central bankers are now forced to weigh the inflationary impulse from higher energy against the risk that more restrictive policy could eventually slow growth more sharply.[13][14][30] For equity investors the implication is that factor performance may continue to rotate rapidly between growth, value, and defensive segments as the market attempts to price in both earnings durability and shifting discount rates.

Looking ahead to next week, the focus will swing decisively toward the Federal Reserve’s June policy meeting and the associated dot plot, along with any incremental labor and inflation data that could influence the trajectory of rates.[13][17] The Fed has already signaled a cautious approach, and markets broadly expect no change in the policy rate at the June 16–17 meeting, but the tone of the statement and press conference will be critical for assessing whether officials lean more hawkish in light of the recent upside surprises in jobs and inflation.[13][17][28][30] At the same time, investors will be watching the upcoming SpaceX IPO and the newly filed Anthropic IPO as sentiment barometers for the AI and private‑market complex, particularly after last week’s drawdown raised questions about whether public‑market enthusiasm for AI has overshot near‑term fundamentals.[18][29][30] In this environment, we expect positioning to remain more tactical, with systematic and discretionary players alike reducing gross exposure, rotating selectively toward quality within growth, and maintaining optionality through higher cash balances or overlays until there is more clarity on both the Fed and the sustainability of AI‑driven earnings revisions.[13][14][31]

value_picks.name: Campbell Soup Company
value_picks.why_undervalued: Campbell Soup is trading at roughly half of its 52‑week high and at a steep discount to Morningstar’s fair value estimate of 55, despite being highlighted as one of the most affordable value stocks in the market.[9][11] Its current price around 22 dollars versus a fair value near 55 implies a valuation gap of well over 50%, even before considering the defensive nature of its cash flows.[9][11] The stock’s price‑to‑earnings ratio in the low double digits is below what investors have historically paid for stable, branded packaged‑food franchises, suggesting considerable multiple compression. The market appears to be extrapolating near‑term volume and mix headwinds, as well as concerns about private‑label competition, into perpetuity rather than recognizing the durability of Campbell’s brands and distribution network. This pessimism has left the shares priced more like a structurally impaired business than a century‑old staple franchise with recurring demand.[9][11]
value_picks.bull_case: The bull case centers on Campbell’s ability to stabilize volumes, push through targeted pricing, and leverage cost savings to translate modest top‑line growth into outsized free cash flow conversion.[9][11] As inflation moderates and promotional intensity normalizes, margin recovery could drive earnings and cash flow growth faster than revenues, providing a natural catalyst for a re‑rating toward historical valuation multiples. Management has been sharpening the portfolio toward higher‑margin categories and leveraging scale in procurement and manufacturing, which should support structurally higher profitability. If investors regain confidence that Campbell’s can sustain mid‑single‑digit earnings growth while maintaining a healthy dividend, the stock could move closer to its estimated fair value range, closing much of the current discount.[9][11] Any strategic actions such as accretive bolt‑on acquisitions or further portfolio pruning would add optionality to the equity story.
value_picks.why_could_go_lower: The bear case is that secular shifts in consumer preferences and retailer shelf strategies could erode the long‑term relevance of legacy canned soup and packaged foods, limiting the company’s ability to grow volumes in real terms.[9][11] If private labels continue to gain share and retailers use their leverage to squeeze branded manufacturers, Campbell’s pricing power and margins could prove weaker than expected. Cost inflation spikes or execution missteps on supply‑chain initiatives could further pressure profitability, causing investors to doubt the sustainability of the dividend and cash flows. In such a scenario, the current low multiple may reflect a more permanent structural decline rather than a temporary dislocation, allowing the stock to languish near its lows or drift even lower.[9][11]

value_picks.name: General Mills, Inc.
value_picks.why_undervalued: General Mills is trading just above its 52‑week low and at roughly 40% below its recent high, even though its trailing free cash flow yield of 9.2% is well above its historical average of 6.8%.[20][28] A single‑digit price‑to‑earnings multiple for a diversified portfolio of consumer staples brands with strong cash generation suggests a valuation more consistent with a highly cyclical or structurally challenged business than a defensive compounder.[20][28] The market appears to be discounting concerns about volume elasticities after price hikes, changing consumer tastes, and retailer pushback to an extreme degree. This has resulted in a situation where investors are being paid an unusually high cash flow yield to hold a business whose end‑market demand has historically been resilient through economic cycles. The combination of depressed multiples, elevated FCF yield, and proximity to the 52‑week low indicates that General Mills is significantly mispriced relative to its intrinsic cash‑generating capacity.[20][28]
value_picks.bull_case: The bull case is that as price and mix effects anniversary and consumers adjust, volume headwinds will moderate, allowing General Mills to stabilize or modestly grow revenues while protecting margins.[20][28] Management’s focus on productivity, cost discipline, and portfolio reshaping toward higher‑growth and higher‑margin segments should support robust free cash flow, even in a low‑growth environment. With a nearly 10% free cash flow yield versus a historical range in the mid‑single digits, there is ample room for a re‑rating if investors come to see current conditions as cyclical rather than structural.[28] As the company continues returning capital via dividends and buybacks, per‑share value creation could be meaningful, especially if sentiment toward consumer staples improves as investors seek defensive yield. Any upside surprises in innovation, international expansion, or margin resilience could accelerate the closing of the valuation gap.
value_picks.why_could_go_lower: The principal risk is that shifting consumer preferences away from processed and packaged foods toward fresher, private‑label, or niche brands could persistently pressure General Mills’ volumes and pricing power. If large retailers prioritize private labels or exact greater concessions on trade spend, the company may see continued mix and margin pressure that undermines the investment case. Elevated leverage relative to some peers could become a concern if operating performance weakens, potentially constraining capital returns or strategic flexibility.[20] In a prolonged inflationary environment, further input cost pressures might not be fully recoverable through pricing, leading to structurally lower margins and validating the market’s cautious stance. Under such circumstances, today’s low multiple could prove justified or even generous, and the stock could continue to drift around or below current levels.

value_picks.name: Kohl's Corporation
value_picks.why_undervalued: Kohl’s trades at a mid‑single‑digit earnings multiple and less than 2 billion dollars in market capitalization, despite generating on the order of 600 million dollars of adjusted free cash flow in a normalized year and reducing net debt to around 760 million dollars.[13][17] The market is effectively valuing the equity at roughly 3 times this normalized free cash flow, a level typically associated with distressed or melting‑ice‑cube situations. Recent analysis highlights that cash is up roughly 500 million dollars and debt is down about 400 million dollars, indicating active balance‑sheet repair that is not reflected in the valuation.[13] At the same time, the stock offers a double‑digit dividend yield, which indicates that investors are pricing in a high probability of a cut or structural decline in earnings.[17] This combination of low multiple, tangible deleveraging progress, and still‑profitable operations suggests the shares are priced far below a conservative estimate of going‑concern value.
value_picks.bull_case: The bull case rests on Kohl’s ability to stabilize comparable sales, improve inventory productivity, and continue cost discipline, allowing it to sustain several hundred million dollars of annual free cash flow.[13] With net debt already under a billion dollars and trending lower, the balance sheet provides room for the company to navigate a challenging retail environment while preserving optionality.[13] If management can execute on merchandising, loyalty, and omnichannel initiatives, even low‑single‑digit sales growth combined with modest margin expansion would justify a higher valuation multiple. The current dividend yield provides a significant current return, and even a partial re‑rating to a high single‑digit or low double‑digit free cash flow multiple would imply meaningful upside from current levels.[13][17] Additionally, any strategic interest from financial or strategic buyers, or real estate value realization, could highlight the disconnect between the stock price and the underlying asset value.
value_picks.why_could_go_lower: The key bear thesis is that department store traffic and mid‑market apparel retail are in long‑term secular decline, and Kohl’s may be unable to offset this with digital growth or differentiated merchandising. If comparable sales continue to erode, fixed‑cost deleveraging could pressure margins and compress free cash flow, making the current dividend unsustainable and forcing a cut that would remove a major support for the stock.[13][17] Intensifying competition from off‑price, specialty, and e‑commerce players could further commoditize Kohl’s assortment and erode its pricing power. In a recessionary scenario, discretionary spending could weaken materially, and credit losses or promotional activity might spike, exacerbating pressure on profitability. Under such circumstances, the market could come to view Kohl’s as a value trap, and the stock could retest its 52‑week low or even move lower as investors question the long‑term viability of the format.[13][17]

value_picks.name: PVH Corp.
value_picks.why_undervalued: PVH is trading roughly 20–25% below its 52‑week high despite reporting fourth‑quarter 2025 revenue and earnings above guidance and guiding to stable operating margins with revenue projected to increase slightly in 2026.[23][26] The company has materially de‑risked its balance sheet, with debt‑to‑equity under 1x, yet the market continues to apply a discount more typical of highly levered or structurally impaired apparel names.[23][26] Investors appear overly focused on macro concerns around discretionary spending, wholesale channel volatility, and fashion risk, while underappreciating the strength of the Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger brands and the company’s margin discipline. The current valuation embeds a skeptical view that PVH can translate brand equity and operational improvements into sustained free cash flow growth. This skepticism creates an opportunity if the company merely delivers on its modest guidance and continues to refine its brand and channel mix.
value_picks.bull_case: The bull case is that PVH’s focus on its core global brands, disciplined inventory management, and cost control enables it to sustain stable or improving margins even in a choppy macro environment.[26] As the company leans into direct‑to‑consumer and higher‑margin channels, mix improvements could support earnings and cash flow growth ahead of low single‑digit revenue growth. A cleaner balance sheet with sub‑1x debt‑to‑equity enhances financial flexibility and lowers equity risk, which over time should warrant a higher valuation multiple more in line with global branded apparel peers.[23] If management continues to beat or at least meet its conservative guidance, investor confidence in the durability of the business model could rise, compressing the discount to peers and to its own historical averages. Any acceleration in consumer demand, favorable fashion cycles, or strategic actions around underperforming segments would provide additional upside catalysts.[23][26]
value_picks.why_could_go_lower: The main risk is that PVH operates in a highly competitive and cyclical apparel market where consumer tastes can shift quickly, and even strong brands can lose relevance if execution falters.[23][26] A slowdown in global discretionary spending, particularly in Europe or North America, could pressure volumes and force higher promotional activity, compressing margins. If wholesale partners continue to rationalize inventory or floor space, PVH might face ongoing channel disruption that offsets gains in direct‑to‑consumer. Currency volatility and geopolitical risks in key sourcing and selling regions could create additional earnings noise, which a cautious market might interpret as structural rather than cyclical. In such a scenario, investors could assign a persistently low multiple to PVH’s earnings and cash flows, and the stock might struggle to re‑rate or could drift closer to its 52‑week low.[23][26]

value_picks.name: The Clorox Company
value_picks.why_undervalued: Clorox shares trade roughly 25–30% below their 52‑week high and near the lower end of their one‑year range, following a period of margin pressure and a cybersecurity incident that weighed on sentiment.[21][27] Despite these issues, the company retains a portfolio of leading cleaning and household brands with resilient demand characteristics, yet it now trades on a mid‑teens earnings multiple that is low relative to its own pre‑pandemic history. Analysts’ average price target of about 104.58 dollars sits modestly above the current price, suggesting that the sell‑off may have overshot near‑term fundamentals.[21][27] The market seems to be extrapolating recent cost pressures, volume normalization post‑pandemic, and execution risks around supply‑chain restoration into a structurally weaker margin profile. This has left the shares valued more like a no‑growth, structurally impaired staple than a branded franchise with potential for margin recovery and steady cash generation.[21][27]
value_picks.bull_case: The bull case is that Clorox successfully executes on its cost savings and pricing initiatives, allowing gross and operating margins to recover toward historical levels as supply‑chain disruptions fade. As input cost inflation moderates, the benefits of prior price increases could flow more fully to the bottom line, expanding earnings and free cash flow. The company’s leading share in core cleaning categories and ongoing product innovation provide a base for modest volume and mix growth over the medium term. If Clorox can demonstrate a few quarters of consistent margin and earnings improvement, investors may reassess the durability of the franchise and be willing to pay a higher multiple more in line with historical norms. The current valuation offers room for such a re‑rating, particularly if management continues to prioritize debt reduction and shareholder returns through dividends.[21][27]
value_picks.why_could_go_lower: The bear case is that competitive pressures from private labels and other branded peers, combined with changing consumer habits post‑pandemic, could limit Clorox’s ability to sustain elevated pricing without sacrificing volume. If cost savings and efficiency initiatives underdeliver, margins might remain structurally below pre‑pandemic levels, making current earnings power less attractive than it appears. Continued execution risks in supply chain and IT, including any lingering effects of prior cybersecurity issues, could create further volatility in results and erode investor confidence.[21][27] In addition, if interest rates remain higher for longer, defensive yield names like Clorox might face multiple compression as income‑oriented investors find alternatives in fixed income. Under these circumstances, the stock could remain range‑bound near the lower end of its 52‑week band or drift lower as investors question whether the business can return to its former profitability profile.[21][27]

momentum_picks.risk_reward: From current levels, the risk/reward profile is skewed toward investors who believe that XPO can continue to execute on operational improvements and gain share in a still-fragmented LTL market, as the market is rewarding the company for visible self-help levers rather than purely cyclical volume growth.[23] If XPO delivers on its targeted margin expansion and maintains pricing power even as freight markets normalize, the present valuation could prove reasonable relative to its earnings growth trajectory, leaving room for further upside over a multi-quarter horizon.[23] However, to justify additional multiple expansion, the company likely needs to continue beating and raising guidance, which makes future quarters more execution-sensitive than in the past.
momentum_picks.key_risks: The primary risk to the momentum thesis is that freight demand could soften more than expected in a macro slowdown, pressuring volumes and limiting the company’s ability to sustain recent pricing gains, which would quickly show up in margin compression.[23] XPO also faces industry competition and potential labor cost pressures, and any misstep in integrating network improvements or technology rollouts could disrupt service levels and damage the brand at a time when expectations are elevated.[23] Finally, because the stock has recently rerated on strong results and positive sentiment, any earnings miss or cautious forward guidance could trigger a sharp reversal as momentum-oriented investors exit.

risks.risk: US CPI release and inflation momentum
risks.impact: The upcoming Consumer Price Index release will be the first major test of whether the recent firming in inflation is transitory or represents a more persistent re-acceleration, following a 0.6% monthly gain in April and a 3.8% year-on-year increase in the CPI-U.[31] A hotter-than-expected print would likely push real yields higher across the curve, pressure growth and AI-linked equities, and reinforce market expectations that the Fed will postpone any rate cuts, while a downside surprise could catalyze a relief rally in duration-sensitive segments.[26][25] Equity investors should watch the breadth of any post-CPI move, particularly whether small caps and cyclicals participate or whether the reaction remains narrowly focused in long-duration tech and communication services.

narrative:
# AI Whiplash And Higher-For-Longer: US Equity Strategy Weekly

## Market Overview

US equities entered a more volatile regime over the past week, as an abrupt reversal in the artificial intelligence and semiconductor complex intersected with a higher‑for‑longer repricing of Federal Reserve policy and a renewed energy‑driven inflation scare.[13][20][30][31] After grinding to fresh record highs at the start of June, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite suffered their sharpest single‑day declines of 2026 on Friday, led by high‑beta AI and chip names that had been the prime beneficiaries of the past year’s multiple expansion.[6][20][30][31] The S&P 500’s latest reported close around 7,405 still leaves the index up robustly year‑to‑date, but the path has become far choppier as investors question how much of the AI earnings story has already been discounted into prices.[1][8][31] The Nasdaq Composite, which has been even more levered to AI enthusiasm and mega‑cap growth, similarly remains elevated near 25,700, but the first week of June saw the Nasdaq 100 fall about 4.5%, underperforming the S&P 500’s roughly 2.4% decline as the AI trade finally encountered meaningful profit‑taking.[2][31]

Early in the week, the prevailing narrative still centered on AI euphoria. On June 2, the S&P 500 notched yet another record close, with the index edging higher on the back of strength in semiconductors and AI‑linked names, including a notable surge in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index of more than 5% intraday.[8] Broad market breadth looked healthier at that point, with the Russell 2000 small‑cap index outperforming on the day and defensive sectors like utilities also advancing, suggesting that systematic trend‑following and retail flows were fully engaged.[8] Investor attention was squarely focused on AI infrastructure winners, with Hewlett Packard Enterprise rallying nearly 20% on the day after a strong earnings print tied to AI data‑center demand, and Marvell Technology gaining roughly 30% at one point during the week on optimism about its positioning in data‑center networking and custom accelerators.[8][18] This phase culminated in a series of record closes for the major indices, underpinned by an assumption that AI‑related capital expenditures and profit growth could run unabated for multiple years.[8][11][18]

The tone shifted dramatically by week’s end. On Friday, a combination of macro and micro catalysts triggered what several observers described as the biggest equity sell‑off of 2026 so far, with the S&P 500 down about 2.6% and the Nasdaq Composite off more than 4% on the day.[6][20][25][30] The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged more than 10%, led by sharp declines in Micron Technology, Broadcom, Marvell Technology, and Advanced Micro Devices, each of which fell in the mid‑single‑to high‑single‑digit range as investors reassessed lofty expectations embedded in AI‑sensitive earnings forecasts.[20][26][30] Social and financial media pointed to a market‑wide loss of roughly 1.8 trillion dollars in equity capitalization on the day, underscoring how crowded the AI trade had become and how quickly sentiment can reverse when valuation and positioning are stretched.[25][30][31] Volatility, as measured by the VIX index, spiked by more than 30% over the week and roughly 24% over the prior five days, signaling a regime shift from the unusually low realized and implied volatility that had characterized much of the year.[30]

Macro data and policy expectations amplified the risk‑off move rather than cushioning it. The latest US payrolls report showed a gain of around 172,000 jobs in May, far exceeding consensus expectations near 88,000 and marking the third consecutive upside surprise in monthly employment growth.[30] At the same time, the unemployment rate ticked up to roughly 4.3%, highlighting late‑cycle dynamics where labor markets are no longer tightening but also not weakening enough to give the Federal Reserve confidence that inflation pressures will subside quickly.[30] The Fed’s preferred inflation measure, the personal consumption expenditures price index, is running around 3.8% year‑over‑year as of April, up from about 3.5% in March and well above the 2% target, keeping officials firmly in a data‑dependent but cautious stance.[28][30] As a result, policy rates remain in a 3.50%–3.75% target range after the Fed paused its late‑2025 easing cycle, and futures markets now price less than a 10% probability of any rate cuts in 2026, with odds of a rate hike by year end creeping modestly higher.[13]

This macro backdrop has pushed major strategists, including Goldman Sachs, to push out their expectations for rate cuts. Goldman now projects that the Fed will not begin its next leg of easing until June 2027, followed by another cut in December 2027, compared with a prior baseline that had cuts beginning in late 2026.[14] The rationale rests on the combination of resilient real activity, a still‑healthy labor market, and inflation that has proven stickier than anticipated when adjusted for energy, housing, and wage dynamics.[14][28] For equity markets, this translates into a higher discount rate applied to future cash flows, which is particularly challenging for long‑duration growth assets such as high‑multiple software and AI infrastructure plays. The convergence of that higher‑for‑longer narrative with signs of speculative excess in AI‑adjacent equities is what made last week’s price action feel like a regime inflection rather than a garden‑variety pullback.[13][14][30]

Geopolitics and commodities layered an additional complication on top of this evolving macro‑market interaction. Renewed conflict in the Middle East, with reports of resumed bombing exchanges between Iran and Israel, pushed Brent crude prices sharply higher toward the upper double‑digit range and raised the prospect of a renewed energy‑driven inflation impulse just as central banks are trying to guide inflation back to target.[30] Analysts noted that the increase in oil prices, if sustained, could add to headline inflation readings over the coming quarters and potentially seep into core measures via transportation and production costs, complicating the Fed’s already delicate balancing act.[13][14][30] Equity markets responded with a modest rotation into energy and select materials names, but the primary effect was to increase uncertainty rather than to catalyze a decisive shift into traditional inflation hedges. Combined with the AI valuation reset and the higher‑for‑longer repricing, the result is an equity market that is still near its highs in level terms but increasingly fragile beneath the surface.

## Sector Leadership & Rotation

The most striking feature of the past week’s trading was the violent sector rotation away from the prior AI‑driven leaders in technology and communication services toward a more defensive and value‑tilted mix, even though the magnitude of the move was not uniform across the GICS spectrum.[18][20][30][31] Technology, which had been the clear outperformer year‑to‑date on the back of strength in semiconductors, cloud, and AI infrastructure, suffered a sudden drawdown as the semiconductor complex sold off and investors questioned the sustainability of the recent surge in AI‑related capital expenditures.[18][20][26][31] Names such as Broadcom, Marvell Technology, Advanced Micro Devices, and Micron Technology led the decline within semis, while some of the AI‑exposed software and infrastructure names, including data‑center and cybersecurity stocks, also traded lower, albeit with somewhat more resilience where earnings support was strongest.[20][21][31] Despite the pullback, the broader technology sector still commands a premium valuation relative to history, and the recent price action is better described as a sharp multiple compression and sentiment reset than as a fully fledged de‑rating of the AI theme.

Within communication services, the picture was more nuanced. Mega‑cap platforms such as Alphabet and Meta have recently reported exceptionally strong quarters, with Alphabet’s Google Cloud segment accelerating to 63% year‑over‑year revenue growth and Meta delivering its fastest revenue growth in four years, around 33% year‑on‑year, driven in large part by LLM‑scale improvements in ad targeting and content recommendations.[11][32] These fundamentals provided some cushion for the stocks during the broader AI selloff, and Alphabet in particular managed to hold in relatively better than some of its mega‑cap peers immediately post‑earnings.[11][32] However, as AI valuations in the hardware and infrastructure layer came under scrutiny, investors began to scrutinize how much of the AI‑driven ad monetization upside is already embedded in these platforms’ share prices. As a result, even fundamentally solid communication services leaders were not fully immune to the de‑risking, with volatility rising and options markets pricing fatter tails in both directions.[11][31]

Energy emerged as a relative winner over the week, benefiting from the surge in oil prices tied to renewed geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and concerns about potential supply disruptions.[30][31] Integrated producers, upstream exploration and production companies, and energy‑services names all attracted incremental flows as investors sought hedges against the possibility that higher oil could extend the duration of above‑target inflation.[30] Historically, episodes of rising energy prices related to geopolitical shocks have produced short bursts of sector outperformance followed by normalization as supply routes adjust, but this time the interaction with AI‑driven capex cycles and higher‑for‑longer monetary policy leaves the medium‑term outlook more complex.[13][14][30] For now, the main takeaway is that the correlation structure between energy and growth has shifted: energy has regained its role as both an inflation hedge and a macro hedge, while tech has shifted from being a defensive growth haven to a locus of speculative excess and de‑risking.

Financials experienced cross‑currents stemming from the same macro forces but responded more benignly than long‑duration growth sectors. On the one hand, expectations that the Fed will keep rates higher for longer, combined with resilient labor and activity data, support net‑interest margins for banks and the earnings outlook for insurers and asset managers.[13][14][30] On the other hand, an acceleration in equity volatility and the risk of further drawdowns in richly valued segments pose mark‑to‑market risks for trading‑oriented franchises and wealth management businesses.[13][31] Large money‑center banks and diversified financials, including names such as JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and Bank of America, appear reasonably positioned in this environment, with capital levels robust and credit losses still manageable, but multiple expansion is likely capped until there is more clarity on the path of policy and credit quality.[13][14]

Healthcare and consumer staples played their traditional roles as relative defensives in the latter part of the week as investors sought out earnings stability and lower beta exposures. While there were no major idiosyncratic developments in the largest managed‑care or pharmaceutical names over the week, the sector’s lower sensitivity to the AI cycle and interest‑rate expectations made it a natural recipient of rotation away from crowded growth trades.[31] Similarly, large consumer‑staples companies and branded food and beverage players saw more resilient price action as their cash‑flow visibility and dividend support remain attractive in a choppier tape, even if their secular growth prospects lack the excitement of AI.[31] The outperformance of these defensive sectors was not dramatic in level terms, but the improvement in relative performance ratios and factor returns suggests that systematic strategies are beginning to rebuild exposure after a prolonged period of underweighting.

Industrials, materials, and real estate each delivered mixed signals. Industrials with exposure to energy, defense, and infrastructure enjoyed some tailwinds from the combination of higher commodity prices and still‑solid public‑spending outlooks, while more cyclical transportation and manufacturing names traded in line with the broader market.[18][30][31] Materials were caught between stronger demand for energy‑related and data‑center‑related inputs on the one hand, and concerns about global growth—particularly in Asia, where South Korea’s KOSPI fell more than 7% and Japan’s Nikkei dropped nearly 4% in the latest selloff—on the other.[30][33] Real estate, especially rate‑sensitive REITs, struggled with the higher‑for‑longer rate repricing and the associated pressure on cap rates, although the move was more contained than in some earlier rate shocks given that much of the structural bear case for certain commercial real estate segments is already well understood and priced.[13][14] Overall, the sector rotation picture is one of late‑cycle dynamics: growth leadership is intact but wobbling, defensives are stabilizing, and cyclicals are trading idiosyncratically based on commodity and policy cross‑currents.

## Macro & Rates Environment

The macro backdrop for US equities is best characterized as late‑cycle resilience colliding with persistent inflation and rising policy uncertainty. The May payrolls report, showing job growth of roughly 172,000 versus expectations near 88,000, marked the third consecutive upside surprise in monthly employment gains and suggested that the labor market remains fundamentally healthy even as the pace of improvement slows.[30] The three‑month average of private payrolls has climbed to its highest level since mid‑2023 after dipping close to stall speed earlier in the year, reinforcing the view that the economy is not on the cusp of recession despite mounting concerns about policy tightness.[30] At the same time, the unemployment rate has moved up toward roughly 4.3%, reflecting a modest increase from cycle lows but still consistent with a strong labor market by historical standards, particularly when viewed alongside continued wage growth and steady labor‑force participation.[30]

Inflation dynamics remain the key constraint on policy. The personal consumption expenditures price index, which the Fed uses as its primary inflation gauge, is running at about 3.8% year‑over‑year as of April, up from roughly 3.5% in March, with core measures also holding above target despite some progress from peak levels.[28][30] This stickiness reflects a combination of factors, including shelter costs that have been slow to adjust, services inflation driven by wage growth, and episodic shocks from energy and geopolitical developments.[28][30] The latest flare‑up in the Middle East and the associated rise in Brent crude prices toward the high‑double‑digit range risks adding another leg to headline inflation, and potentially to core if higher transportation and production costs feed through more broadly.[30] From the Fed’s perspective, this mix of resilient growth and stubborn inflation argues strongly for a cautious stance and a willingness to tolerate restrictive policy settings for longer than markets had previously expected.

Against this backdrop, the Federal Reserve has left its target federal funds rate unchanged at 3.50%–3.75% for three consecutive meetings in January, March, and April 2026, following an earlier easing cycle that began in late 2025.[13] Futures markets now imply virtually no chance of a rate cut at the upcoming June meeting, and less than a 10% probability of any cut over the balance of 2026, with some non‑trivial odds that the next policy move could actually be a hike if inflation surprises materially to the upside.[13] Goldman Sachs Research has adjusted its outlook accordingly, no longer expecting rate reductions in late 2026 and instead projecting the next two cuts in June and December 2027, which would bring the policy rate back toward a 3.0%–3.25% terminal range.[14] Importantly, Goldman also notes that while further hikes are not their base case, the bar for renewed tightening has fallen somewhat as the economy has proven more resilient than expected and inflation progress has stalled, even if only modestly.[14]

The Fed’s communication challenge has been compounded by institutional uncertainty. Earlier this year, the Federal Reserve Chair, Jerome Powell, disclosed that the Department of Justice had served the Fed with grand jury subpoenas related to his prior testimony before Congress, an unprecedented development that has raised questions about central bank independence in some quarters.[27] While Powell emphasized that no individual, including the Fed chair, is above the law and that the institution would cooperate fully, the optics of a criminal investigation touching on the Fed’s leadership have fed into a broader political debate about monetary policy, inflation, and accountability.[27][30] Concurrently, market commentators have highlighted the potential for changes in Fed leadership or composition, including speculation around former Fed governor Kevin Warsh’s role in the policy debate, to influence the balance of risks between inflation and growth objectives.[13][27] For markets, the key point is that the path of policy is subject not only to economic data but also to evolving institutional dynamics that may alter the Fed’s reaction function at the margin.

The next major macro event on the calendar is the Federal Open Market Committee’s June 16–17 meeting, where officials are widely expected to leave the policy rate unchanged but could adjust their forward guidance and updated Summary of Economic Projections.[13][17] Market‑implied probabilities, as reflected in fed‑funds futures, suggest near‑unanimous expectations for a hold at this meeting, but investors will parse the dot plot for clues about the likely number and timing of future cuts—or hikes—through 2027.[13][14][17] Given the recent upside surprises in payrolls and the re‑acceleration of the PCE inflation gauge, there is a meaningful risk that officials revise up their estimates of the appropriate policy path, effectively endorsing the higher‑for‑longer narrative that markets have begun to price.[13][14][28] The tone of the Chair’s press conference will also be critical, particularly any commentary on the balance of risks between inflation and growth, the potential impact of renewed energy price shocks, and the interaction between policy and elevated valuations in AI‑sensitive equity sectors.

Internationally, cross‑currents from Asia and Europe are feeding back into US asset prices via risk sentiment and trade channels. The recent global selloff saw South Korea’s KOSPI index drop more than 7% in a single session, Japan’s Nikkei 225 fall nearly 4%, and China’s CSI 300 decline over 2%, reflecting both local growth concerns and the global de‑risking from AI and semiconductor names that are heavily represented in Asian indices.[30][33] Europe’s Stoxx 600 and the UK’s FTSE 100 also traded lower, though less dramatically, as rising oil prices and renewed geopolitical tensions weighed on sentiment.[30] For US investors, these moves underscore that the AI and semiconductor cycle is global, not just a US phenomenon, and that any sustained correction in these themes will reverberate through multiple geographies and supply chains.

The most important macro catalyst is the Federal Reserve’s June 16–17 FOMC meeting, where officials will decide on the appropriate level of the federal funds rate and update their projections for growth, inflation, and the policy path.[13][17] Markets overwhelmingly expect no change in the policy rate at this meeting, but the updated dot plot and the Chair’s press conference will be scrutinized for any signs of a more hawkish tilt in response to recent upside surprises in payrolls and inflation.[13][14][28] Given the heightened sensitivity of AI and other long‑duration growth equities to interest‑rate expectations, any upward shift in the median projected policy path for 2026–2027 could spark further volatility and sector rotation.

Inflation data releases, including upcoming CPI and PCE prints, remain critical, even though exact release dates are not specified in the week’s public sources. The latest PCE reading of about 3.8% year‑over‑year in April underscores that inflation progress has stalled somewhat, and investors will be watching for signs of re‑acceleration or renewed disinflation in subsequent months.[28][30] A downside surprise in core inflation would provide the Fed with more flexibility and could support a rebound in long‑duration growth assets, while an upside surprise would reinforce the higher‑for‑longer narrative and potentially pressure valuations further.[13][14][28]

On the event‑driven side, the forthcoming IPOs of SpaceX and Anthropic are likely to be key sentiment drivers for the AI and growth complex. Fortune and Bloomberg reporting indicate that SpaceX’s IPO is multiple times oversubscribed, with intense interest from both institutional and retail investors, while Anthropic’s confidential filing and near‑trillion‑dollar valuation underscore the extraordinary appetite for AI pure‑plays.[18][29][30] The timing of these offerings appears to be imminent, with commentary noting that the SpaceX IPO is expected on a Friday shortly after the latest selloff, but exact dates are not publicly pinned down in the sources.[29][30] Strong post‑IPO performance would likely rekindle enthusiasm for AI equities and support high valuations across the ecosystem, while disappointing outcomes could reinforce fears of an AI bubble and accelerate the rotation into value and defensives.

Earnings season is currently between major waves for our watchlist, but select names will continue to report over the coming weeks. CrowdStrike’s recent earnings demonstrate that cybersecurity demand remains robust, and subsequent reports from peers such as Zscaler, Palo Alto Networks, and others will help clarify whether this strength is broad‑based or idiosyncratic.[21][31] In software and AI infrastructure, upcoming results from data‑platform, observability, and developer‑tooling companies will shed light on the pace at which AI experimentation is translating into production workloads and recurring revenues. Financials, energy, and materials will also provide incremental color about the health of the real economy, the impact of higher energy prices, and the state of credit and capital expenditure cycles.

Finally, index and benchmark events such as the revised Russell reconstitution, which is moving from an annual to a semi‑annual schedule starting in 2026, will create technical flows that can affect smaller‑cap and mid‑cap names on our watchlist.[4] The timing and composition of these reconstitutions influence index‑tracking and factor‑based strategies, potentially generating short‑term dislocations and liquidity events in affected stocks.[4][31] For active managers, these events represent both risks and opportunities, as they can temporarily decouple prices from fundamentals and allow for more attractive entry or exit points.

## What To Watch Next Week

As we look to the coming week, the key question for US equities is whether last week’s AI‑driven selloff marks the beginning of a more sustained de‑risking or merely a sharp but ultimately contained reset in an ongoing bull market. The answer will depend on three interlocking factors: the evolution of the macro data and Fed communication, the behavior of AI‑linked earnings revisions and capex guidance, and the resilience of investor risk appetite in the face of heightened volatility.

On the macro side, any incremental labor, inflation, or activity data that feed into the Fed’s reaction function will be critical. Markets are currently aligned with a higher‑for‑longer narrative, with futures pricing implying little chance of cuts in 2026 and even some odds of a hike, but there remains substantial uncertainty about how the Fed will respond if growth slows more meaningfully while inflation remains above target.[13][14][30] The June FOMC meeting will therefore be a major inflection point, and we expect trading in rates‑sensitive sectors—including high‑multiple growth, financials, and real estate—to remain choppy into and immediately after the decision.[13][17]

Within the AI complex, we will be watching closely for any sign that companies begin to temper their capex plans or that customers signal a more cautious approach to AI‑related spending. Thus far, cloud hyperscalers and major platforms have continued to ramp AI infrastructure investments aggressively, with capex guidance increasing by tens of billions of dollars across the largest players, but last week’s price action may prompt more probing questions from investors and analysts about returns on invested capital and the timing of monetization.[11][31][32] Any shift in tone on AI capex from management teams—whether in formal guidance, conference presentations, or informal commentary—could have outsized impacts on stocks across the AI value chain.

Investor positioning and risk appetite constitute the third pillar of our near‑term outlook. The spike in the VIX and the sharp moves in semiconductors and AI infrastructure suggest that leverage and crowding had built up in these trades, and we suspect that deleveraging among hedge funds and systematic strategies is still in progress.[30][31][33] However, the fact that S&P futures bounced modestly in pre‑market trading following Friday’s selloff, and that retail and passive flows remain largely intact, indicates that there is still substantial underlying demand for equities, particularly on dips.[30][31] The interplay between forced sellers and opportunistic buyers will determine whether volatility remains elevated or begins to subside as the market digests the latest macro and micro information.

From a portfolio‑construction perspective, we advocate maintaining exposure to high‑quality AI beneficiaries with demonstrable earnings power and strong balance sheets, while reducing concentration in the most speculative and crowded parts of the theme. Within our watchlist, this argues for core positions in mega‑cap platforms and diversified AI infrastructure names, balanced by increased allocations to defensives such as healthcare and staples, as well as selective exposure to energy and materials as hedges against inflation and geopolitical risk.[11][13][14][18][30] Risk management should emphasize scenario analysis around different policy and growth outcomes, options‑based hedges where appropriate, and careful liquidity planning ahead of known catalysts such as the June FOMC meeting and major AI‑related IPOs.

In sum, US equities remain in a constructive but more fragile regime. The AI revolution is real and increasingly visible in earnings, but the market’s ability to capitalize on it will depend on the interplay between fundamentals, policy, and positioning. The coming weeks will be critical in determining whether the recent turbulence represents a pause that refreshes or an early warning of a more significant regime shift in the equity landscape.[11][13][14][18][30][31]
